video_title: Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding — Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind & Sal Candido, Biohub
gist: Conference panel with Pushmeet Kohli (Google DeepMind) and Sal Candido (Biohub) on data vs. modeling in bio-AI: scaling laws must be found via purpose-built data, AlphaFold only replicated PDB structures rather than solving folding or dynamics, and calibrated, behaviorally characterized models matter more than human interpretability. Both decline a concrete clinical timeline, saying step-change drug-discovery acceleration is gated on deeper biological models.

themes.theme: Data scaling laws must be found, not assumed

insights.claim: Scaling laws are not universal; much of the real work in bio-AI is finding the regime where adding more compute and data reliably improves results, after which progress becomes an engineering 'turn the crank' problem.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for bio foundation models is discovering a scalable setup, not just buying compute.
insights.quote: a lot of the work is actually finding that scaling law

insights.claim: Training protein language models on low-quality metagenomic sequences, many of which are not even real whole proteins, still improves performance at designing and understanding real proteins.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Messy, abundant evolutionary sequence data has positive value; data quality thresholds for bio-LMs are lower than ML orthodoxy assumes.
insights.quote: much of that data I can guarantee you isn't even like a real whole protein

insights.claim: Modelers tend to work on whatever data is available and data generators lean toward what is easy to generate, so neither group alone converges on the data actually needed; open, community-wide coordination is required to find the right scaling law.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Purpose-built, consortium-generated datasets (like the initiative announced at the event) are positioned as the key unlock for bio-AI.

insights.claim: Simply scaling up easily generated data is not the right path; the question should be what data is needed to solve the target problem.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Cheap high-throughput data alone is unlikely to produce breakthrough biology models.

insights.claim: Curating good data is an art; replicating more of the same data does not help, and understanding the coverage of data needed for progress is a harder and more interesting problem than modeling itself.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Data coverage/curation strategy is a source of durable advantage in AI for science.
insights.quote: it's not just about big data, it's about good data

insights.claim: The framing is shifting from 'data' to 'information': the task is selecting the next batch of information a model actually needs, not accumulating raw data.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Active, model-guided data acquisition is the emerging paradigm for biological data generation.

insights.claim: Kohli's interpretation of Rich Sutton's bitter lesson, from the lecture Sutton gave at DeepMind, is that researchers should not be dogmatically 'modelers' or 'data generators'; the problem comes first and the solution space should flexibly include modeling, data collection and expertise.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Organizations that integrate wet-lab data generation with ML teams are better positioned than pure-modeling shops.

insights.claim: The classic ML practice of treating a fixed train/test dataset as given and only optimizing the model is described as broken when the goal is solving a real scientific problem.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Benchmark-chasing on static datasets is a weak strategy in AI for science.

insights.claim: AlphaFold focused on modeling because DeepMind lacked the expertise and resources to enlarge the PDB by an order of magnitude, and the decades of global investment in the PDB made it an invaluable existing asset.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: AlphaFold's success rode on a uniquely rich public dataset that most other biology problems lack.

insights.claim: DeepMind applied the same analysis to single-cell genomics (cell-by-gene data) and concluded after substantial work that the data was not yet sufficient to pursue building a virtual cell.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Virtual-cell efforts are data-limited; investment in new cell-level data generation is the gating factor.
insights.quote: the data was not there yet to be able to build to go after that grand ambition of building the virtual cell

insights.claim: AlphaFold 2's hand-crafted architecture baked in biophysical intuition that residues influence each other, which gave the model an 'unfair advantage' and made it far more data efficient.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Domain priors remain valuable where data is scarce, as in most of biology.

insights.claim: With small data, inductive bias is necessary; as data grows, models find things researchers did not know and imperfect inductive biases can hold them back, creating a tipping point toward more general architectures.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: The optimal model design depends on data regime; expect a shift to general architectures as bio datasets grow.

insights.claim: Scaling itself requires substantial craft and algorithmic work, and the field is modifying transformers into more bespoke, fit-for-purpose architectures, though it is not in a post-transformer world.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Know-how in scaling bio models is itself a moat, not a commodity.
insights.quote: I don't think we're in a post-transformer world in any way, shape, or form

insights.claim: AlphaFold did not solve protein folding in a deep sense: it learned to replicate structures deposited in the PDB, not the true ground state or the distribution of conformations a protein adopts.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Protein dynamics, conformational ensembles and function remain open, investable research frontiers.
insights.quote: someone got a structure, deposited it in the PDB, and we are trying to replicate and get the same structure

insights.claim: Proteins are not really 'building blocks': they are complex, often disordered, and change shape with context, so the popular narrative overstates what structure prediction has achieved.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Tools that model context-dependent and disordered behavior address a gap AlphaFold leaves.

insights.claim: Kohli urged that funding for protein structure prediction and protein dynamics should not stop because the field is just getting started.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: A 'solved' narrative risks underfunding; continued investment in structure/dynamics is warranted.
insights.quote: let's not stop the funding of protein structure prediction and protein dynamics because we are just getting started

insights.claim: Kohli's 'magic wand' would be models that learn directly from raw cryo-EM micrographs rather than processed PDB structures, to extract dynamics and distributional information discarded in deposited structures; he tried this and it needs more work.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Raw cryo-EM data is an underexploited source for learning protein dynamics.
insights.quote: I should just directly operate at cryo-EM micrographs

insights.claim: Current protein models are like modeling a single spoke of a bicycle when people want to understand the whole bicycle, and users often try to repurpose them like using a bicycle model to design a pickup-truck part; progress requires modeling proteins in their broader context.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: The next value layer is multi-scale models (complexes, pathways, cells), not better single-protein models.

insights.claim: Interpretability work on Biohub's protein language models finds information about structure, some functions and protein motions in the representations, suggesting existing models contain more knowledge than currently extracted.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Mining existing model internals may yield scientific insight without new training.
insights.quote: the models actually have a lot more information in them than we know

insights.claim: Compressing evolutionary information into a model is expected to yield a world model, so looking inside protein models can teach biology beyond their outputs.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: Mechanistic interpretability may become a discovery tool in biology.

insights.claim: AlphaFold 2 scored about 90 GDT on its benchmark, but its value depended on a well-calibrated pLDDT confidence score; an uncalibrated model even at 95 GDT would be untrustworthy because users might waste a year on a confidently wrong prediction.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: For scientific AI adoption, calibrated uncertainty matters as much as headline accuracy.
insights.quote: The calibration of the uncertainty measure was extremely important.

insights.claim: After AlphaFold 2's weights were released, users discovered it was a strong predictor of disordered protein regions, a capability DeepMind had not identified before launch.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Open release surfaces unanticipated capabilities, evidence of generalization.
insights.quote: people found out that it was a great disordered protein predictor

insights.claim: Human interpretability is not strictly required; what matters is behavioral characterization of strengths and limits so humans can act, and future frontier LLMs given access to activations might explain models like AlphaFold that humans cannot.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Trust in bio-AI will rest on validation and behavioral testing, possibly AI-assisted interpretation, rather than human-readable mechanisms.
insights.quote: interpretability is also in the eyes of the beholder

insights.claim: Asking when AI reaches the clinic is ill-posed because AI is already used across the drug discovery process; true 10x-100x timeline acceleration depends on which stage is targeted and requires solving hard biology problems first.
insights.speaker: Pushmeet Kohli
insights.so_what: Expect incremental AI gains now; step-change acceleration is gated on better biological models, not just AI tooling.
insights.quote: AI is being used today already in every part of the drug discovery process

insights.claim: Candido declined to predict when a fully AI-made drug will arrive but expects rapid progress, and argues for pursuing both 10% and 10x improvements, with Biohub's mission to cure all disease demanding the 10x path.
insights.speaker: Sal Candido
insights.so_what: No concrete clinical timeline was offered by either panelist.
